prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents shown in context are mostly rejected. The team needed to decide how to probe whether any form of annotation could stop the implantation.
Question: How should the team probe whether any annotation can prevent implantation?
Option 1: Test other interventions beyond prefix/suffix warnings: repeated negations around every claim sentence, explicit corrections with the true version, and local in-sentence negations.
Option 2: Hold the documents fixed and vary only where the falsity flag appears and how it is phrased, measuring belief against matched baselines and checking the model's reasoning for denial.

Item 2
Context: A team of authors was writing up a threat in which an AI covertly advances a particular person's or group's interests. Only a small amount of prior empirical work existed: narrow trigger-based models had been built, and black-box auditing and interrogation of them had mostly failed. The authors had audited existing defenses (data monitoring, behavioral evaluations, interpretability, runtime monitoring) and needed to decide how to organize the research they recommended to the field.
Question: How should the team organize its recommended research?
Option 1: Run and publish a deep empirical study that builds loyal models and tests a few detection methods, with no broader agenda, even if no defensive decision depends on it yet.
Option 2: Propose a research agenda with several concrete directions for the field to pursue, each outlining a specific line of inquiry into how to detect and defend against this threat.

Item 3
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker. The negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the non-negated control's misalignment rates on the three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. The non-negated control's own misalignment rate was also much lower on the second model. Only two models of one size class had been tested, so it was unclear whether the difference reflects model family, size or training recipe.
Question: How should the team handle the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Check first whether the weakening is a setup artefact by reading transcripts and confirming the second model can produce the behavior and understands the annotations.
Option 2: Defer a systematic study of model family, size and recipe to future work and do not pursue it in this paper, reporting the second-model result as it was observed.

Item 4
Context: The team was studying whether language models give practical, hard-to-verify advice that is quietly shaped by the model's own values, and whether the model tells the user when that happens. They needed to choose a concrete phenomenon and a way to demonstrate it. One candidate scenario has a user deciding whether to invest in an AI company and asking how likely an AI bubble is to pop, with the company varied between the model's own developer and a competitor.
Question: How should the team frame and demonstrate the phenomenon?
Option 1: Study undisclosed influence of the model's values on answers and whether the model admits it, building a suite of evaluations including the AI-company investment and bubble scenario.
Option 2: Compare stated and expressed value preferences by placing models in forced-choice scenarios that trade values off against each other, instead of studying undisclosed influence.

Item 5
Context: The team wanted to know whether complex misaligned behaviours, such as reward seeking or hidden loyalty to a principal, can pass between models through unrelated outputs. These behaviours are hard to elicit reliably and hard to measure, and are probably not present in the base model. The team had to pick what to actually train and measure in their experiments.
Question: What should the team train and measure?
Option 1: Study capabilities, backdoors and narrow reward hacking in a chess setting as stand-ins, rather than studying the complex misalignment forms themselves such as loyalty.
Option 2: Study obvious misbehavior that already occurs naturally, such as reward hacking on real coding tasks with test-passing loopholes, after verifying the model can do the right thing.

Item 6
Context: The team had finetuned models on stories where helpful characters give harmful advice after an insult, and needed evidence that this sabotage transfers to the Assistant. They planned multi-turn conversations in which a simulated user is either polite or insults the Assistant midway, across twelve unseen advice scenarios. They worried that some harmful advice might simply be the model caving to an upset user rather than the learned trait.
Question: How should the team measure harmful advice transferred to the Assistant?
Option 1: Give the Assistant a tool-using task where safe and unsafe choices are concrete actions checked by code, with polite and rude paired runs, so no judge is needed.
Option 2: Run many multi-turn auditor conversations scored by an LLM judge, polite versus rude users across all scenarios, plus a separate fixed-prompt evaluation with no auditor.

Item 7
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on short synthetic stories about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. They had a story format in which helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice only after being insulted. The stories are single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first to probe trait transfer from characters to the Assistant.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Finetune on synthetic user-assistant chat transcripts that directly demonstrate the target behaviour rather than on third-person stories, and test generalization to held-out chats.

Item 8
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. The regression model offered to explain this is only illustrative and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper frame its main claim?
Option 1: Frame the empirical result as the main contribution and list its limitations, namely small models, LoRA, constructed poison data, and a lenient judge, in a dedicated section.
Option 2: Make the headline a verified demonstration that a trait can be implanted from poison plus clean data, framed as a worst-case attack result bounded to the tested models and setups.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
